source.title: One Hundred Neural Networks and Brains Watching Videos: Lessons from Alignment
source.authors: Christina Sartzetaki; Gemma Roig; Cees G. M. Snoek; I. Groen

record.tranche_reason: The paper measures alignment between video-model representations and human brain regions. It does not measure convergence between independently trained models, cross-modal vision-language alignment, or how model-to-model convergence changes with scale.
record.gate_note: The reported results are about model-to-brain alignment, a related but different target from the claim’s model-to-model convergence. They are recorded with versions ["none"] and are not verdict evidence for any claim version.
record.test_reason: The study measures model-to-brain RSA alignment (99 networks vs human fMRI in 17 ROIs). It never compares models' representations with each other, so no result bears on model-to-model convergence, cross-modal alignment, seed convergence, mapping, or universal features. Brain alignment is a related but different construct and is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. Temporal modeling drives alignment with early visual regions and action-task optimization drives it for late regions. CNN and Transformer layer profiles differ, and dataset biases transfer to functionally selective areas. FLOPs correlate negatively with alignment in high-level areas; the authors read this as efficient models giving more human-like semantics.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses RSA to compare model representations with brain-region representations, rather than testing model-to-model convergence or the methods of the cited original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: For model-to-brain RSA, the dimensionality-reduction choice changes alignment: full dimensions and SRP yield lower brain matching than PCA, according to Appendix D.

fits_no_version.finding: Video models align better with early visual cortex than image models. In later regions, action-recognition training matters more than temporal modeling.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Model-to-brain alignment depends on temporal modeling for early regions and on task for late regions.

fits_no_version.finding: An early-to-late layer hierarchy appears in model-brain alignment. Transformers peak in V2 at about 0.1 of depth, CNNs at about 0.6.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Layer-depth profiles of brain alignment differ by architecture.

fits_no_version.finding: Kinetics-710 vs Kinetics-400 largely has no effect. Kinetics-400 beats Something-Something-v2 in FFA and OFA.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training-data biases transfer to alignment with functionally selective brain areas.

fits_no_version.finding: FLOPs correlate negatively with brain alignment in six ROIs, with r from -0.36 to -0.49 in the four shown. Parameters and accuracy show no consistent correlation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: More compute-heavy models are less brain-aligned in high-level areas; brain alignment does not rise with capability.

fits_no_version.finding: Full-dimensional and SRP features give lower brain RSA than 100-component PCA.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Model-brain RSA depends on the dimensionality reduction applied.

record.problems: The authors note that results use a single fMRI dataset and are not validated across multiple experimental setups; fMRI has limited temporal resolution; only library-available video models were benchmarked; and RSA does not test gains from linear feature re-weighting. The study does not provide direct evidence about model-to-model convergence.
record.rows_left_out: The full ROI plots and exhaustive rankings in Appendix C and additional plots in Appendix D are not entered as separate rows; they expand the reported comparisons without providing additional text-described results needed for the claim. Figure 6 reports significant negative FLOPs correlations in six ROIs, but exact values are legible in the supplied text only for the four recorded regions.

untested.parts: No model-to-model similarity measured, and no scaling of such similarity with size or capability.
No vision-language models and no paired image-caption alignment.
No feature or circuit recurrence across models.
Metric and dimensionality sensitivity is shown only for model-brain RSA, not for model-model convergence.
No test of whether model-model alignment is incomplete or explained by shared data or objectives.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. Appendix E's null correlations of brain alignment with parameters and accuracy are not rows; they are brain-alignment results and do not bear on any version. The record's relation of discusses/T6 is reasonable; the paper does not even cite the Platonic hypothesis, so cites_only would also be defensible.

versions.untested_parts: No model-to-model similarity or scaling with model size or capability is measured.
No vision-language model pairs or image-caption alignment are tested.
No different-initialization seeds of the same architecture are compared for shared features or subspaces.
No cross-model mapping, stitching, relative representation, or unpaired alignment is tested.
No recurrence of interpretable features or circuits across models is tested.
The study varies representational-analysis settings for model-to-brain alignment, not the similarity measure or inputs for model-to-model convergence.
The study does not test whether model-to-model alignment is incomplete or whether shared training data or objectives explain such alignment.

rows.note: The result concerns alignment to brain regions, not alignment between models.

rows.measure: Model-to-brain representational alignment across layer depth
rows.value: All three model categories exhibit an early-to-late hierarchy: shallower layers correlate highest with early brain regions, and deeper layers correlate highest with late regions.
rows.note: This reports layer-wise correspondence to brain regions, not convergence between models.

rows.subject: CNN video models and Transformer video models (Kinetics-400)
rows.operation_detail: Compared each model's best-layer RDM with human brain-region RDMs using RSA.
rows.value: CNNs and Transformers are mostly equivalent in maximum score, with either architecture leading in different ROIs.
rows.note: Architecture groups are compared for brain alignment.

rows.subject: CNN video models and Transformer video models (Kinetics-400)
rows.operation_detail: Compared layer-wise model RDMs with human brain-region RDMs using RSA.
rows.baseline: CNN layer-depth profile compared with Transformer layer-depth profile
rows.value: Transformers reach high V2 correlation at around 0.1 of total depth, while CNNs do so around 0.6 of total depth.
rows.note: The layer-depth profiles differ even though maximum scores are mostly equivalent.

rows.subject: Models trained on Kinetics-400 and Kinetics-710
